title: The Cherry Orchard
author: Anton Chekhov
note: Julius West’s English of Chekhov’s 1904 play — a Russian estate in blossom, a merchant with a plan, and a family that cannot bear to sell the trees. Project Gutenberg 7986. Opens at ACT ONE.

scenes.title: ACT ONE
scenes.reentry: [A room which is still called the nursery.
scenes.prompt: Who still belongs to this house?

breaths.text: [A room which is still called the nursery.
One of the doors leads into ANYA’S room.
It is close on sunrise.
It is May.
The cherry-trees are in flower but it is chilly in the garden.
There is an early frost.
The windows of the room are shut.
DUNYASHA comes in with a candle, and LOPAKHIN with a book in his hand.]
Lopakhin: The train’s arrived, thank God.
Lopakhin: What’s the time?
Dunyasha: It will soon be two.
Dunyasha: [Blows out candle] It is light already.
Lopakhin: How much was the train late?
Lopakhin: Two hours at least.
Lopakhin: [Yawns and stretches himself] I have made a rotten mess of it!
Lopakhin: I came here on purpose to meet them at the station, and then overslept myself... in my chair.
Lopakhin: It’s a pity.
Lopakhin: I wish you’d wakened me.
Dunyasha: I thought you’d gone away.
Dunyasha: [Listening] I think I hear them coming.
Lopakhin: [Listens] No....
Lopakhin: They’ve got to collect their luggage and so on....
Lopakhin: [Pause] Lubov Andreyevna has been living abroad for five years; I don’t know what she’ll be like now....
Lopakhin: She’s a good sort--an easy, simple person.
Lopakhin: I remember when I was a boy of fifteen, my father, who is dead--he used to keep a shop in the village here--hit me on the face with his fist, and my nose bled....
Lopakhin: We had gone into the yard together for something or other, and he was a little drunk.
Lopakhin: Lubov Andreyevna, as I remember her now, was still young, and very thin, and she took me to the washstand here in this very room, the nursery.
Lopakhin: She said, “Don’t cry, little man, it’ll be all right in time for your wedding.”
Lopakhin: [Pause] “Little man”....
Lopakhin: My father was a peasant, it’s true, but here I am in a white waistcoat and yellow shoes... a pearl out of an oyster.
Lopakhin: I’m rich now, with lots of money, but just think about it and examine me, and you’ll find I’m still a peasant down to the marrow of my bones.
Lopakhin: [Turns over the pages of his book] Here I’ve been reading this book, but I understood nothing.
Lopakhin: I read and fell asleep.
[Pause.]
Dunyasha: The dogs didn’t sleep all night; they know that they’re coming.
Lopakhin: What’s up with you, Dunyasha...?
Dunyasha: My hands are shaking.
Dunyasha: I shall faint.
Lopakhin: You’re too sensitive, Dunyasha.
Lopakhin: You dress just like a lady, and you do your hair like one too.
Lopakhin: You oughtn’t.
Lopakhin: You should know your place.
[Enters with a bouquet.
He wears a short jacket and brilliantly polished boots which squeak audibly.
Epikhodov: He drops the bouquet as he enters, then picks it up] The gardener sent these; says they’re to go into the dining-room.
[Gives the bouquet to DUNYASHA.]
Lopakhin: And you’ll bring me some kvass.
Dunyasha: Very well.
[Exit.]
Epikhodov: There’s a frost this morning--three degrees, and the cherry-trees are all in flower.
Epikhodov: I can’t approve of our climate.
Epikhodov: [Sighs] I can’t.
Epikhodov: Our climate is indisposed to favour us even this once.
Epikhodov: And, Ermolai Alexeyevitch, allow me to say to you, in addition, that I bought myself some boots two days ago, and I beg to assure you that they squeak in a perfectly unbearable manner.
Epikhodov: What shall I put on them?
Lopakhin: Go away.
Lopakhin: You bore me.
Epikhodov: Some misfortune happens to me every day.
Epikhodov: But I don’t complain; I’m used to it, and I can smile.
Epikhodov: [DUNYASHA comes in and brings LOPAKHIN some kvass] I shall go.
Epikhodov: [Knocks over a chair] There....
Epikhodov: [Triumphantly] There, you see, if I may use the word, what circumstances I am in, so to speak.
Epikhodov: It is even simply marvellous.
[Exit.]
Dunyasha: I may confess to you, Ermolai Alexeyevitch, that Epikhodov has proposed to me.
Lopakhin: Ah!
Dunyasha: I don’t know what to do about it.
Dunyasha: He’s a nice young man, but every now and again, when he begins talking, you can’t understand a word he’s saying.
Dunyasha: I think I like him.
Dunyasha: He’s madly in love with me.
Dunyasha: He’s an unlucky man; every day something happens.
Dunyasha: We tease him about it.
Dunyasha: They call him “Two-and-twenty troubles.”
Lopakhin: [Listens] There they come, I think.
Dunyasha: They’re coming!
Dunyasha: What’s the matter with me?
Dunyasha: I’m cold all over.
Lopakhin: There they are, right enough.
Lopakhin: Let’s go and meet them.
Lopakhin: Will she know me?
Lopakhin: We haven’t seen each other for five years.
Dunyasha: [Excited] I shall faint in a minute....
Dunyasha: Oh, I’m fainting!
[Two carriages are heard driving up to the house.
LOPAKHIN and DUNYASHA quickly go out.
The stage is empty.
A noise begins in the next room.
FIERS, leaning on a stick, walks quickly across the stage; he has just been to meet LUBOV ANDREYEVNA.
He wears an old-fashioned livery and a tall hat.
He is saying something to himself, but not a word of it can be made out.
The noise behind the stage gets louder and louder.
A voice is heard: “Let’s go in there.”
Enter LUBOV ANDREYEVNA, ANYA, and CHARLOTTA IVANOVNA with a little dog on a chain, and all dressed in travelling clothes, VARYA in a long coat and with a kerchief on her head.
GAEV, SIMEONOV-PISCHIN, LOPAKHIN, DUNYASHA with a parcel and an umbrella, and a servant with luggage--all cross the room.]
Anya: Let’s come through here.
Anya: Do you remember what this room is, mother?
